paras: The Ensley Alley H house dynamiting was the bombing of a house occupied by Black residents at Alley H and Twenty-first street in Ensley, Alabama, on Thursday, August 19, 1920. The blast wrecked the house and injured two of its occupants, but no one was killed. The Birmingham Age-Herald first presented it as one of a series of unsolved dynamitings, then reported that police had arrested a Black man who blew up the house to avenge himself on his estranged wife, while a Black-press wire brief said the dynamiters had not been caught.

Ensley had seen earlier blasts that month, including the dynamiting of the store and house of Tony Antonio, an Italian merchant on Avenue F. The Age-Herald's first report counted three attempts to blow up houses in Ensley in three weeks, while its second counted the Alley H blast as the second in ten days.

According to the first Age-Herald report, the explosion came about 2 o'clock on Thursday afternoon, wrecked two rooms and left only one or two walls standing on the other side of the house. That report said two Black men who lived in the house were seriously injured and taken to the emergency hospital at Ensley.

The paper's account the next day put the blast at 2 o'clock Thursday morning and said the dynamite had been placed under the room of Melissa Mitchell and her twelve-year-old son, destroying the floor and furniture of the two-room house. In this version mother and son, who "escaped death by a miracle," were taken to the Ensley infirmary shocked but only slightly hurt, and two women in the rear room were unhurt.

On the day after the blast, officers investigating said they had found no clue to a motive. By August 21 the Age-Herald reported that Officers Millicen and Tyler had arrested Coleman McShants, a Black man, and placed him in the Ensley jail, and that he was "said to have confessed." Police attributed the blast to revenge after McShants and his wife had separated. No report of a charge, indictment or trial for McShants was found in the coverage.

The Birmingham Age-Herald covered the blast twice in local columns, first under the headline "DYNAMITERS REPEAT BUT LEAVE NO CLUE," which grouped it with other Ensley bombings. Its second story, "NEGRO DYNAMITES HOUSE FOR REVENGE," recast the event as a domestic quarrel and relayed the police account of a confession without attribution beyond "is said to have."

In the Black press the event appeared as a two-sentence brief from the Associated Negro Press, printed on September 4 in the Cleveland Advocate under an Ensley dateline of September 1 and in the Tulsa Star, dated September 3, under the heading "Dynamite Colored Residence." The brief described the target as "the home of a Colored family," said it had been dynamited for the second time in two weeks, and closed by noting that police had been unable to capture the dynamiters. It made no mention of the arrest or the revenge motive reported in Birmingham.

The two Age-Herald reports disagree on the hour of the blast, on who was hurt and how badly, and on whether the culprit was known. The later account names the occupants and gives a motive, but it rests on police statements about a confession. The Black-press brief, written about two weeks later, says the dynamiters were still at large and that the home had been bombed twice, so it may describe a second blast at the same address rather than the August 19 one.

reader.title: Ensley Alley H house dynamiting
bases: Every report describes a dwelling occupied by Black residents blown up with dynamite, with injuries but no deaths (A2, A3, A4, A5).

Two Age-Herald reports and a Black-press brief agree that a house occupied by Black residents at Alley H in Ensley was dynamited on a Thursday (A2, A3, A4, A5), though they disagree on the time, the injured and the culprit.

accounts.label: Age-Herald first report
accounts.gist: A house occupied by Black residents was nearly wrecked about 2 o'clock Thursday afternoon, two Black men living there were seriously hurt, and officers had no clue to a motive; it was the latest of three attempts to blow up houses in Ensley in three weeks.

accounts.label: Ensley police (Age-Herald, next day)
accounts.gist: Coleman McShants, a Black man separated from his wife, blew up the house at 2 a.m. Thursday for revenge and confessed; Melissa Mitchell and her son were slightly hurt and two women in the rear room were unhurt.

accounts.label: Black-press brief (A.N.P.)
accounts.gist: For the second time in two weeks the home of a Black family at Alley H and Twenty-first street was dynamited 'last Thursday morning', and police had not captured the dynamiters.

framing.detail: The Age-Herald first framed the blast as part of a series ('DYNAMITERS REPEAT BUT LEAVE NO CLUE'), then a day later as a private act of revenge ('NEGRO DYNAMITES HOUSE FOR REVENGE ... By Jealous Husband'), relaying the police version.
A short wire item headed 'Dynamite Colored Residence' stressed a repeated attack on a Black home and the failure of police to catch anyone, without mentioning an arrest or motive.

conflicts.note: The Black-press brief also says 'Thursday morning'; the Age-Herald's first report may have misread the hour.
